how_it_wins:
You have four ways to end the game, and a checker has signed all four. Two of them are unbounded. Stack 009 loops Warren Soultrader, Gravecrawler and Bastion of Remembrance, and each activation's Treasure funds the next cast exactly. Stack 011 runs the same recursion through Phyrexian Altar, pays nothing at all, and gains you a life every time round.

The other two are lethal and they stop — for different reasons, and the difference is worth carrying to the table. Stack 012 is Exquisite Blood beside a body that reads "Whenever you gain life, each opponent loses 1 life." Once lit it is mandatory, and it is not a draw precisely because every cycle takes a life from every seat: drain #40 empties the pod. That one is lethal because it ends.

Stack 010 ends for a different reason — your own library. It needs 39 activations to zero the table against the 59 the mandatory draw permits, a margin of 20. All four kills take four opponents from 40 to 0 at the same moment. You are not winning a seat. You are winning the table.

Here is the part most pilots get backwards, so get it right from turn one: your commander is not the plan. Three of the four verified kills never name him. Yawgmoth is a mana-free instant-speed sacrifice outlet stapled to a draw engine, and that is a magnificent job — he arrives on turn 4 in 7,220 of 10,000 goldfished games, mean 4.294, 91.1% by turn 6. Use him to draw for three or four turns. Let the table spend removal on him. Then win with something he was never part of.

The enabler layers are deep and the kills are thin, and that split is the whole pilot's manual. By turn 10, unassisted, you have drawn a drain 82.4% of the time, a free repeatable sacrifice outlet 77.9%, renewable fodder 73.6%, an ignition source 73.1%, engine mana 61.9%, one of five tutors 60.6%. The specific kills read much smaller — KILL A 1.1% unassisted and 18.0% with a tutor, KILL B 0.5% / 12.3%, KILL C 6.9% / 42.5%, KILL D 4.6% / 33.7% (goldfish_metrics.json, 10,000 iterations, seed 42). Read those one at a time and never add them together; the simulator scores each requirement group on its own and there is no figure in it that means "any kill assembled." What the split tells you is simple: you will almost always have the machine running. Your job is to find the one missing piece, which is exactly what five tutors are for.

What beats you is not a wrath. A wrath is a payoff here — Bastion of Remembrance, Zulaport Cutthroat, Blood Artist and The Meathook Massacre all drain when your creatures die, and 28 creature copies plus Gravecrawler and Reassembling Skeleton rebuild cheaper than anyone at the table. What beats you is a permanent you cannot remove. deck-audit measures interaction-breadth at 2 answered classes against a target of 5, with no detected answer to artifacts, graveyards or lands, while every kill you have is a small pile of permanents sitting in the open. So deploy in the order that costs you least when it is answered, keep the drain in hand until the turn it converts, and present the assembly when the table's mana is spent. Bracket floor is 4 on four Game Changers and eleven two-card infinite records; say that out loud at Rule 0 and then go play the deck it describes.

combo_lines.002: Relish the target restriction first: Yawgmoth's ability reads "up to one target creature," and the Insect that Nest of Scarabs is about to make does not exist yet when you choose. Protection from Humans bars him from pointing at himself, so once the opponent's body is gone every legal target is one of your own tokens — two bodies out, one back. The holding: exactly five completed activations, seven of your creatures dead, 28 life removed from a pod of 160, and your own life going up. This is a value engine that draws you five cards. It is not a kill, and no ordering makes it one.
combo_lines.003: Three clauses do the work here, and each one is a permission rather than a restriction: an activation is cost-paid (CR 113.3b), you choose which creature pays "Sacrifice another creature" (CR 601.2h), and "up to one target" lets you choose none at all (CR 115.6). Put together, they mean nothing on this board can take Zulaport Cutthroat away from you against your will — he survives every iteration and is spent only as the deliberate last sacrifice, where his own leaves-the-battlefield trigger looks back and banks the seventh drain. The holding: five activations plus one proliferate, seven drains, each opponent down 7, 28 across the table. Not lethal, and worth knowing before you commit to it as a plan.
combo_lines.004: The whole case turns on four words. Blood Artist says "target player loses 1 life" — one seat per trigger, chosen when the trigger goes on the stack — where the drains that close games say each opponent. On this board the engine ends by eating its own payoff, because Yawgmoth's protection from Humans bars him as a target and "another creature" bars him as the sacrifice, leaving Blood Artist as the last legal thing to point at. The holding: eight creature deaths, eight triggers, eight life removed of 160. Short by 152. When you are choosing which drain to deploy, this is the arithmetic that decides it.
combo_lines.005: The precise point is that gaining zero is not gaining. CR 119.9 means an event that gains you 0 life is not a life-gain event at all, so when an Insect dies to its own -1/-1 counter at toughness 0, South Wind Avatar's dies-trigger resolves for nothing and its second ability never fires. The holding: eight completed activations, eight dies-triggers, but only seven drains — 28 opposing life, each opponent 40 to 33, ended by having no body left to sacrifice. The Avatar's 4 toughness is what buys the last four activations, so its size is doing real work even on a board where a bigger body usually is not.
combo_lines.006: The rule you want is CR 122.6, and it is broader than it looks: a reference to counters being put on an object covers an object that is given counters as it enters, not only counters placed on something already sitting there. Persist names no player, so 122.6a makes you the one putting the counter on, which satisfies Nest of Scarabs' "whenever you put one or more -1/-1 counters on a creature." The holding: yes, the Nest triggers, and you get an Insect — even though the returned Fume Spitter enters as a 0/0 and is in the graveyard again before that trigger reaches the stack. The trigger had already triggered. Reanimating a one-toughness creature is still a token.
combo_lines.008: Savour the sequencing: the sacrifice is an activation cost, paid after the ability is already the topmost object on the stack (CR 602.2a into 601.2h), so the trigger it causes lands above the ability and resolves first. That is why one Yawgmoth activation paid with a token pays Mirkwood Bats twice — once for the sacrifice now, once for the creation two resolutions later. The holding on this board: thirteen Bats triggers, each opponent 40 to 27, 52 life removed. One caution the stack itself insists on and you should carry to the table: this is a creation-and-sacrifice drainer on its own board, and its figure is not interchangeable with what a death-metered drain does on a different one.
combo_lines.009: The elegant clause is CR 113.6f — an ability that modifies which zone its own card may be cast from functions in that zone — so Gravecrawler's permission is live in the graveyard on every single iteration, with the Zombie condition met by Warren Soultrader, whom the loop never eats because the cost says "another creature." The Treasure each activation makes is an artifact, not a creature, so it pays for the recast without restriction. The holding: the loop is self-funding and unbounded. Per completed iteration your life is net 0 with a floor of 39, each opponent is -1, and your Treasure count is unchanged. Thirty-nine further iterations take all four opponents to 0 at once.
combo_lines.010: The crux is CR 704.5q: if a permanent has both a +1/+1 and a -1/-1 counter, state-based actions remove one of each. So the counter Yawgmoth puts on an undying body does not shrink it — it strips the +1/+1 that undying left behind and re-arms the creature to die again. The holding: the alternation is real, but the loop is finite. It needs 39 further activations and the mandatory draw caps you at 59, a margin of 20 (up to 25 if you save a free outlet as the finisher). The trap is Viscera Seer: sacrificing mid-loop with her free ability places no counter, and only Yawgmoth's counter can strip an undying return, so a spare sacrifice costs you a body you cannot get back.
combo_lines.011: One line of rules text makes this the cleanest kill in the deck: Phyrexian Altar's ability needs no target and could add mana, so it is a mana ability (CR 605.1a) and never uses the stack (CR 605.3b) — it cannot be responded to, and its {B} is in your pool before anyone gets priority. Sacrificing Gravecrawler to the Altar therefore refunds exactly the mana that recasts him, with Carrion Feeder holding up the Zombie condition and never being the sacrifice. The holding: unbounded, and free. Each completed iteration is +1 life for you and -1 for every opponent. Thirty-nine further iterations put all four at 0 at the same state-based-action check, and you finish at 80.
combo_lines.012: Counsel's favourite kind of question: the loop is mandatory — neither card says "may" — so does the game simply end in a draw? No, and CR 732.1b is why. A draw requires a sequence that could be repeated indefinitely, and this one cannot: every cycle takes 1 life from every opponent, so there is a way to stop, which is all CR 104.4b asks. The holding: drain #40 takes all four opponents from 1 to 0, state-based actions are checked before the resulting triggers reach the stack, and all four leave the game at the same instant (CR 704.5a). You are still there, so you win (CR 104.2a). You end at 80 life, with 117 triggers on the stack that never resolve.

card_roles.Yawgmoth, Thran Physician: A mana-free, instant-speed sacrifice outlet stapled to a draw engine — 'Pay 1 life, Sacrifice another creature' costs no mana at all, which is your best property under a tax or a lock. Pilot him as the card engine he is: three of the four verified kills never name him, and stack 010 is the only one that does.
card_roles.Nest of Scarabs: Turns your commander's removal mode into bodies. Stack 013 settles the arithmetic: the number of creatures you put counters on sets the number of triggers, and the counters on each of those creatures set that trigger's 'that many' — one proliferate across three counter-bearing creatures makes three Insects, not six.
card_roles.Mirkwood Bats: The one drain that is paid on creation as well as sacrifice, which is why stack 008 gets two triggers from a single Yawgmoth activation paid with a token. Its 2/3 body is a genuine consideration on any line that wants small things to die.
card_roles.Ayara, First of Locthwain: A drain on every black creature entering plus a tap-to-draw outlet, and one of the three each-opponent drains the recursion kills accept. {B}{B}{B} is the real cost — she is a turn-3 card only when your first three lands are black, which they usually are.
card_roles.Bastion of Remembrance: The single most load-bearing noncreature permanent you own: three of the four verified kills route their drain through it (stacks 009, 010, 011), and its enters trigger hands you a free Human Soldier to sacrifice. You draw it 16.7% of the time by turn 10 unassisted — hence the tutors.
card_roles.Zulaport Cutthroat: An each-opponent drain on a body, and a legal substitute in the drain slot of every recursion kill. Stack 003 proves the useful thing about him: you are never forced to consume him, so he survives the whole engine and is spent last on purpose.
card_roles.Blood Artist: Drains one target player per trigger rather than each opponent, and stack 004 measured what that costs on a bounded board — eight life removed from a pod of 160. He is still a fine body that pays you for every death; he is simply not the drain you tutor for.
card_roles.South Wind Avatar: Half of stack 012's mandatory two-card kill, and a deathtouch 3/4 whose toughness buys four extra activations on the grinding board (stack 005). Its second ability, 'Whenever you gain life, each opponent loses 1 life,' is the exact text Exquisite Blood needs.
card_roles.Exquisite Blood: One half of the fastest kill you have — mean draw turn 5.301, 6.9% assembled unassisted by turn 10 and 42.5% with a tutor. It needs no sacrifice outlet and touches no graveyard, which makes it the shape to reach for when someone lands graveyard hate.
card_roles.Marauding Blight-Priest: Reads 'Whenever you gain life, each opponent loses 1 life' verbatim — a second body that pairs with Exquisite Blood, and a member of the nine-card drain class the goldfish measures at 82.4% by turn 10.
card_roles.Starscape Cleric: The same each-opponent lifegain trigger on a flier that can't block, with Offspring {2}{B} when you have the mana to buy a second copy of the trigger. Cheap, evasive, and a partner for Exquisite Blood.
card_roles.The Meathook Massacre: Does three jobs on one card: a scalable wipe, an each-opponent drain on your own creatures dying, and lifegain when theirs do. It is the wipe you cast when your board is the one that profits.
card_roles.Grave Pact: Your only repeatable edict, and the answer to a creature you cannot target. Every sacrifice that feeds a drain also makes each of your four opponents give a creature up — one activation, four boards shrinking at once. They pick which one; you just keep sacrificing.
card_roles.Gravecrawler: The card two unbounded kills both route through, and the slot with no substitute. Its own ability modifies the zone it can be cast from (CR 113.6f), so with any Zombie out it recasts itself forever. You see it 16.5% of the time by turn 10 unassisted, 66.5% with a tutor.
card_roles.Warren Soultrader: Stack 009's engine: 'Pay 1 life, Sacrifice another creature: Create a Treasure token,' and the Treasure exactly funds Gravecrawler's next cast. It is also a Zombie, so it satisfies Gravecrawler's condition itself and the loop never has to eat it.
card_roles.Phyrexian Altar: Sacrifice a creature for any colour, as a mana ability that never touches the stack — which is what makes stack 011 free, uncounterable and unbounded. It is the best engine-mana card in the deck by some distance.
card_roles.Pitiless Plunderer: A Treasure for every other creature you lose, which turns a board wipe into a mana pile and any sacrifice engine into a mana engine. Four mana is the price of admission; it earns it on the first activation.
card_roles.Ashnod's Altar: Free sacrifice outlet plus {C}{C}, which powers a lot of things — but note what it cannot do: colorless mana does not cast Gravecrawler for {B}. Use it for outlet and bulk mana, not to fund the recursion loop.
card_roles.Phyrexian Tower: A land that turns a creature into {B}{B}. It is a sacrifice outlet, engine mana and a land drop at once, which is the cheapest kind of card in a deck this tight on slots.
card_roles.Carrion Feeder: A one-mana free sacrifice outlet that is also a Zombie — that dual identity is precisely why stack 011's loop works, since it holds up Gravecrawler's cast permission while never being the thing sacrificed.
card_roles.Viscera Seer: Free outlet, one mana, scry every time. Read stack 010 before you use her mid-loop: her sacrifice places no counter, and only Yawgmoth's counter can strip an undying return, so a spare activation costs a body for good.
card_roles.Woe Strider: Free outlet, a Goat to feed it on arrival, and escape from your own graveyard when the table wipes the board. Three functions on one three-mana card.
card_roles.Yahenni, Undying Partisan: Free outlet with indestructible attached — the one creature you keep through your own sweepers and through most of theirs, and a legal undying body under Mikaeus.
card_roles.Blasting Station: Free outlet that also throws damage, and it untaps whenever a creature enters, which your token production does constantly. It is also a way to close from a board a drain cannot reach.
card_roles.Reassembling Skeleton: Renewable fodder for {1}{B}, over and over, from the graveyard. It never runs out and never asks for anything but mana — the purest form of what this deck wants a body to be.
card_roles.Butcher Ghoul: Undying fodder and a Zombie, so it turns on Gravecrawler and dies twice on its own. Under Mikaeus it is a legal alternation body for stack 010.
card_roles.Geralf's Messenger: Two life from one target opponent on arrival — a single seat, not the pod — plus undying, plus a Zombie for Gravecrawler. {B}{B}{B} is a real ask; the payoff is a body that has to be killed twice.
card_roles.Stitcher's Supplier: A one-mana Zombie that mills on the way in and on the way out, filling the graveyard your recursion suite wants. It also satisfies Gravecrawler's Zombie condition for a single black mana.
card_roles.Bitterblossom: Free fodder every upkeep for 1 life — the cheapest engine in the deck and the one that keeps working while you hold up interaction. Two mana buys you a body a turn for the rest of the game.
card_roles.Grave Titan: Ten power across three bodies on arrival — a 6/6 deathtouch Giant plus two 2/2 Zombies — and two more Zombies every time it attacks. It is the card that makes an empty board into an engine again, and a fine thing to reanimate.
card_roles.Sedgemoor Witch: Ward-pay-3-life makes her hard to remove cheaply, and magecraft turns your instants and sorceries into fodder. Her Pest tokens gain you life when they die, which the lifegain drains notice.
card_roles.Black Market Connections: A Treasure, a card and a 3/2 body every first main phase, priced in life. Take what the board is short of — that flexibility is why it out-earns a fixed draw engine here.
card_roles.Necropotence: Pay 1 life, exile a card, take it at your next end step. In a deck whose loops end at 80 life, life is the cheapest resource you own — spend it early and freely.
card_roles.Skullclamp: One mana, equip one, and any 1/1 you own becomes two cards. With Bitterblossom, Nest of Scarabs and Grave Titan making bodies, this is the deck's most efficient draw.
card_roles.Deadly Dispute: Sacrifice an artifact or creature at instant speed for two cards and a Treasure. It converts a creature in the removal crosshairs into cards and mana rather than nothing.
card_roles.Plumb the Forbidden: Instant-speed insurance: sacrifice as many creatures as you like in response to a wrath or a targeted exile, and copy the spell for each. The taxonomy has no pattern for it, which is not the same as having no function.
card_roles.Sinister Gnarlbark: Draw a card and blight 1 at every end step — a free recurring -1/-1 counter, which means a free recurring Insect with Nest of Scarabs, plus a card. Recurring ignition on a three-mana body.
card_roles.Insatiable Avarice: Spree — {2}{B} in total puts any card on top of your library, {B}{B}{B} draws you three and costs you 3 life, and you may buy both modes on one cast. It is a tutor when you need a piece and raw cards when you need volume.
card_roles.Demonic Tutor: The cleanest card in the format: two mana, any card, straight to hand. When one of your four kills is a piece short, this is the shortest route to it.
card_roles.Vampiric Tutor: Instant-speed, one mana, two life, top of library. It costs a draw step, so cast it on the turn before the turn you need the card.
card_roles.Beseech the Mirror: A tutor that can cast what it finds when bargained — sacrifice an artifact, an enchantment or a token you were going to sacrifice anyway, and the four-or-less piece arrives free.
card_roles.Diabolic Intent: A tutor whose additional cost is exactly what your deck was already going to do. Sacrificing a creature is a payment here and a trigger everywhere else on the board.
card_roles.Persist: Reanimation that returns a nonlegendary creature with a -1/-1 counter, which stack 006 confirms triggers Nest of Scarabs (CR 122.6). Two mana for a body and a token.
card_roles.Victimize: Two creatures back from one sacrifice, tapped. The sacrifice is a death trigger, the returns are two entries — a single card that pays every layer of the engine at once.
card_roles.Animate Dead: Two mana for the best creature in any graveyard, yours or theirs. The -1/-0 rarely matters when the body's job is to be sacrificed.
card_roles.Phyrexian Reclamation: The repeatable graveyard-to-hand route: {1}{B} and 2 life, any number of times, at instant speed. It rebuilds through hate that answers the battlefield rather than the yard.
card_roles.Mikaeus, the Unhallowed: Grants undying to every non-Human you control, which is the whole of stack 010 — the commander's -1/-1 counter annihilates the +1/+1 undying leaves and re-arms the body. Six mana, and worth it.
card_roles.Massacre Girl, Known Killer: Gives your creatures wither, so combat damage becomes -1/-1 counters, and draws you a card whenever an opponent's creature dies with toughness below 1. Removal, ignition and card flow on one body.
card_roles.Skinrender: Three -1/-1 counters on arrival — the deck's best single ignition, since it can kill an opposing creature outright or place three counters on your own body and hand Nest of Scarabs three Insects.
card_roles.Soul Snuffers: A counter on each creature, which sweeps small boards and lights the Nest at the same time. Remember it hits yours too; that is usually a feature, occasionally not.
card_roles.Fume Spitter: One mana, sacrifices itself, places a -1/-1 counter. The cheapest ignition you own and a death trigger in the same card.
card_roles.Black Sun's Zenith: A scalable wipe that places actual counters, which is the only sweeper in the deck that Nest of Scarabs can see. Stack 013 explicitly declines to resolve what X greater than 1 does to the Nest's token count — that one needs a stack scenario before you count on the bigger number.
card_roles.Toxic Deluge: Three mana and X life clears almost anything, including indestructible. It applies -X/-X rather than counters, so the Nest stays quiet — this is your answer, not your engine.
card_roles.Feed the Swarm: The one card in the 99 that destroys a noncreature permanent an opponent controls — and it reads 'creature or enchantment', so an enchantment is the only noncreature it can reach. You draw it 17.3% of the time by turn 10 unassisted; hold it for the permanent that actually stops you.
card_roles.Deadly Rollick: Free while your commander is on the battlefield, and it exiles rather than destroys. The best reason to have Yawgmoth out is often this card.
card_roles.Snuff Out: Free with a Swamp for 4 life — instant-speed removal with no mana, which is how you interact on a turn you spent assembling. It cannot touch a black creature, and in this format that is a real gap.
card_roles.Fatal Push: One mana for mana value 2, or mana value 4 with revolt — and you turn on revolt every time you sacrifice anything, which is constantly. Cheap answers to cheap enablers.
card_roles.Lightning Greaves: Haste and shroud for zero equip, which pulls a commander or a combo piece out of the crosshairs and lets an outlet work the turn it lands. Shroud cuts both ways: you cannot target it either.
card_roles.Supernatural Stamina: Protects a creature from removal and hands you an extra death trigger in the bargain, since the returned body triggers everything again. The role taxonomy has no pattern for it; the function is plain in the text.
card_roles.Gray Merchant of Asphodel: Devotion drain on a Zombie body, and in a mono-black deck full of {B} pips that number gets ugly fast. It is a drain, a Zombie for Gravecrawler and a reanimation target.
card_roles.Sol Ring: Two colorless on turn one, forever. It is the single biggest reason a turn-2 commander happens at all — the goldfish draws fast mana by turn 10 in 42.7% of games unassisted, and Sol Ring is the best card in that group.
card_roles.Ancient Tomb: {C}{C} from a land, and 2 damage to you every time you tap it. Colorless is a real constraint in a deck this black-hungry, but it is the difference between a turn-4 and a turn-2 Yawgmoth.
card_roles.Arcane Signet: Two mana, taps for black, every turn. Unglamorous and correct — it is one of four persistent nonland producers that add black, and with the four rituals it lifts 34 land sources to 42.
card_roles.Dark Ritual: One black into three. The audit does count it — it is one of your eight nonland black sources — but it taps once and is gone. Treat it as a burst that buys one specific turn, and spend it on a turn that matters.
card_roles.Castle Locthwain: A black source that enters untapped when you control a Swamp, plus a repeatable draw for {1}{B}{B}. The life cost scales with your hand, so use it when your hand is small.
card_roles.Cabal Pit: Black mana for 1 damage, and once you hit threshold it sacrifices itself to shrink a creature by 2. A land that becomes removal is exactly the flexibility a linear deck wants.
card_roles.Ifnir Deadlands: Black mana at the cost of a life, plus a late-game sink that puts two -1/-1 counters on an opposing creature. That is removal and Nest ignition from a land slot.
card_roles.Cabal Coffers: '{2}, {T}: Add {B} for each Swamp you control' beside 22 Swamps and Urborg is the largest single mana output in the deck. It counts as one source in the audit; on turn 6 it plays like several.
card_roles.Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth: Makes every land a Swamp, which produces no mana of its own — it counts for zero sources — and turns every land you have into fuel for Cabal Coffers and a Swamp for Snuff Out.
card_roles.Bojuka Bog: Enters tapped, exiles a graveyard on arrival. It is your only graveyard interaction, it costs you nothing but a tapped land, and it is worth holding for the reanimator seat.
card_roles.Takenuma, Abandoned Mire: A black source that channels away to return a creature from your graveyard to hand, cheaper for each legendary creature you control. A land that is also a recursion spell.
card_roles.Command Tower: Untapped black, no cost, no condition. In a mono-black deck it is a Swamp that dodges nothing and asks nothing.
card_roles.Exotic Orchard: Taps for whatever an opponent's lands could make, which in practice means black often enough to count. Untapped and free is the point.
card_roles.City of Brass: Any colour, untapped, for 1 damage a tap. You will pay that damage happily in a deck whose loops end at 80 life.
card_roles.Survivors' Encampment: Colorless, or any colour by tapping a creature you control — and you generally have spare bodies. Just remember tapping a creature is not sacrificing one.
card_roles.Path of Ancestry: Enters tapped for black, and scries when its mana casts a creature that shares a type with Yawgmoth. The tap cost is small in a deck with only three taplands.
card_roles.Agadeem's Awakening // Agadeem, the Unde: A land when you need a land, and a mass reanimation spell when the table has wiped you. Paying 3 life to have it enter untapped is almost always right here.
card_roles.Malakir Rebirth // Malakir Mire: A land on the turns you are short and a two-life save on the turns your key creature is targeted — and the return is another death trigger for everything on your board.
card_roles.Swamp: Twenty-two of them, and they are the reason the black source count works and the reason Cabal Coffers and Snuff Out do what they do. The unglamorous majority of a mana base that hits its turn-3 land drop 91.9% of the time.

mulligan:
Ship freely. The first mulligan is customary and near-free, and you keep your opening seven 81.8% of the time anyway at a mean of 0.216 mulligans across 10,000 goldfished games — the deck is not asking you to gamble on a bad keep.

What you are looking for is not a card, it is a shape: something that sacrifices, something to sacrifice, and lands. In 100-card singleton you mulligan toward classes, not names, and this deck's classes are deep. A free repeatable sacrifice outlet shows up 77.9% of the time by turn 10; renewable fodder 73.6%; an ignition source 73.1%; a drain 82.4%. Carrion Feeder, Viscera Seer, Woe Strider, Blasting Station and Yahenni all do the outlet job. Bitterblossom, Reassembling Skeleton, Stitcher's Supplier and Gravecrawler all do the fodder job. You do not need the specific one.

Keep two to four lands and a cheap enabler. That is the shape of 9,192 of 10,000 kept hands, and the turn-3 land drop lands 91.9% of the time from there. One land is a ship except with Sol Ring, Ancient Tomb or Dark Ritual attached — those three are the whole fast-mana class, and they are in 42.7% of games by turn 10. Zero lands is always a ship; only 288 opening sevens in 10,000 look like that, and none of them play Magic.

Ship the hand that is all payoff. Exquisite Blood, Grave Titan and five lands is a mulligan even though it looks powerful — your mean available mana is 3.911 on turn 4 and 4.603 on turn 5, so a five-drop with nothing before it means you do nothing for half the game. Enablers dig toward payoffs; payoffs sit there until the engine exists. Keep the enabler-heavy hand every time (strategy:mulligans.engine-hands).

Do not mulligan toward your commander. He arrives on turn 4 in 7,220 of 10,000 games and 91.1% by turn 6 without any help from you, and three of the four verified kills never name him. A hand with any of your five tutors is better than a hand with Yawgmoth: 60.6% of games see a tutor by turn 10, and a tutor is how a 1.1% kill becomes an 18.0% one.
upgrades:
Start from where the money actually is. This deck's enabler layers are all north of 60% by turn 10 — a drain at 82.4%, an outlet at 77.9%, fodder at 73.6%, ignition at 73.1%, engine mana at 61.9% — while the four verified kills sit at 1.1%, 0.5%, 6.9% and 4.6% unassisted. That gap is not a flaw to fix by adding a fifth kill. It is the arithmetic of singleton: a named card is 7.1% of an opening seven, so every kill built from named cards will read small, and the lever that moves them is the tutor line and the width of each requirement group. Widening a drain class from three cards to five moves four separate kill rates at once. Adding a sixth combo piece moves one.

Three deck-audit axes read under, and only one of them is real. Card-advantage measures 5 copies against a target of 10, but the audit's own probe names five more cards doing the job that the taxonomy files elsewhere — Ayara, Black Market Connections, Castle Locthwain, Plumb the Forbidden and the commander himself. Protection reads 3 against a 4-6 band with the same caveat. Interaction-breadth reads 2 answered classes against a target of 5, with no detected answer to artifacts, graveyards or lands, and that one holds up: your kills are piles of permanents sitting in the open, and one card in the 99 destroys a noncreature permanent an opponent controls. That is the axis where a slot buys the most.

Sweepers read 4 against a 1-3 cap, which is the least interesting "over" in the report — your own board emptying is a payoff more often than a loss, and you rebuild faster than anyone. Treat that number as headroom rather than a problem. Mana is in the same category: 36 lands and 42 sources both sit at target, so a mana add here has to earn its slot on output rather than on count.

Be sceptical of the obsolescence index on this deck specifically. It flags newer printings for Ashnod's Altar, Phyrexian Altar, Pitiless Plunderer, Carrion Feeder, Mirkwood Bats and Reassembling Skeleton, and its advantages are stat-and-keyword shaped — "Better Power," "Better Toughness," "Lower CMC." A bigger body is not an upgrade in a fodder slot; the thing you are buying is a creature that dies conveniently and comes back. Read the index as a shortlist of cards to look at, never as a verdict about cards to replace.

The bracket ceiling is fixed and generous. The floor is 4, forced independently by four Game Changers and by eleven two-card infinite records, so anything that is not itself a Game Changer changes nothing about the conversation you have at Rule 0. That means the slot math is free: judge each candidate on whether it widens a verified kill's any_of, covers a permanent class you cannot answer, or converts a creature death into mana — and be willing to say no to everything else.
mana_base:
Thirty-six lands across 15 entries, and only three of them enter tapped. Twenty-two are Swamps. That basic count is why Cabal Coffers counts as exactly one black source in the audit and something else entirely at the table — it taps for {B} per Swamp you control, and Urborg turns the rest of your lands into Swamps as well. Three taplands is the number to be pleased about: a deck that wants a creature dying on turn one cannot carry eight of them.

The pip share and the source share agree completely, which almost never happens — black is 100% of the pip load and 100% of the sources. So there is nothing to reconcile, only a count to read: 34 black land sources against the 36 a 90% on-curve rate would take. The audit says out loud what that means, and it is worth quoting — "the target is a yardstick, not a possibility, in a 36-land deck." The whole gap is two lands that produce no black at all: Ancient Tomb, which taps for {C}{C}, and Urborg, which taps for nothing.

That 34 is lands only. Eight nonland sources carry it to 42, and here the audit's own note and its own producer table disagree: the note says "rocks and dorks lift the count to 42", while the eight are Arcane Signet and Phyrexian Altar, Pitiless Plunderer and Warren Soultrader, plus four the taxonomy files as rituals — Dark Ritual, Deadly Dispute, Agadeem's Awakening and Malakir Rebirth. Half the lift comes from a class the phrase does not name. The other half of your rocks does not help either: Sol Ring and Ashnod's Altar add {C}{C} apiece and exactly zero black. Ten ramp pieces in the list, eight of them black sources — that is the honest count.

Of those eight, only Arcane Signet taps for black and asks nothing in return. Phyrexian Altar, Pitiless Plunderer and Warren Soultrader all need a creature to die first, and Agadeem's Awakening and Malakir Rebirth are counted as rituals but arrive as lands off their back faces, which is the truer description of them. So read the jump from 88.2% on lands alone to 95.5% with the rocks and dorks for what it is: seven points bought largely with mana your own engine has to switch on, and the audit takes no survival discount on the creatures holding it up. The goldfish prices the same split — engine mana drawn by turn 10 at 61.9%, fast mana at 42.7%.

The development curve is what a 36-land deck looks like when it is working. You hit your land drop 99.7% of the time on turn 2, 91.9% on turn 3, 80.8% on turn 4, and 58.8% by turn 6. Mean available mana is 3.911 on turn 4 and 5.223 on turn 6; your commander costs four and the goldfish lands him on a median of turn 4, mean 4.294, with 91.1% of games having him down by turn six. The mana base is not the constraint on this deck. It is the part quietly doing its job while you decide which of four kills to assemble.
threat_assessment:
Hold one fact above every other and the whole game reorganises around it: every kill this deck has verified ends all four opponents at the same moment. Stack 009 says 39 further iterations "take all four opponents to 0 at once." Stack 011 says the same and adds "you end at 80 life." Stack 012: "Drain #40 takes all four opponents from 1 to 0 simultaneously." Stack 010: "All four opponents reach 0 together and leave the game; you are still in it, so you win."

That changes what the go decision even is. It is not body arithmetic and it is not "can I get one seat this turn." It is a configuration check.

There are four configurations and you should know them the way you know your own name. Warren Soultrader plus Gravecrawler plus an each-opponent drain (009). Gravecrawler plus Phyrexian Altar plus a second Zombie plus a drain (011). Exquisite Blood plus South Wind Avatar (012). Mikaeus plus your commander plus a non-Human body plus a drain (010). You either hold one of those or you do not, and no amount of extra creatures moves that answer.

So the table never gets a warning turn from you. There is no board state where you are lethal against one seat and merely scary to the rest. You are nothing, and then you are the whole table. Play like it.

Which means the correct way to fear this deck is to audit your permanents for a shape, and almost nobody does that. They count creatures. Goldfish has you at a mean of 3.903 bodies by turn six — a fair-looking swarm, and a swarm is not the plan.

Lean on that mismatch. The commander plus Nest of Scarabs plus a death-metering drain is the board that looks like a kill and is not one: seven drains, 28 life across a four-opponent pod, every seat ending at 33 (stacks 002 and 003, both checker-passed). Mirkwood Bats on that same board is louder still at 13 per opponent and 52 across the pod (stack 008) and it also does not kill anyone. Let them spend answers there. Those are value boards you are happy to have priced as threats.

Now the card the table will never read correctly, and the one you must stop misreading yourself. Gravecrawler is a hidden hub wearing furniture's clothes. It is named in the scenarios of stacks 009, 010 and 011, and it is the recursive half of BOTH unbounded loops — the reason either one is unbounded at all is that it recasts itself from the graveyard for {B} while you control a Zombie.

Goldfish draws it by turn ten in 16.5% of games unassisted and 66.5% with a tutor, mean draw turn 3.764 — and a named card is 7.1% of an opening seven, which is the arithmetic of singleton rather than a defect. Its clothes are perfect: a one-mana 2/1 that cannot block, in a deck full of one-mana 2/1s. Nobody has ever spent removal on it. Deploy it turn one without a flicker of hesitation, because the tell in this deck is never Gravecrawler — it is whatever you play beside it.

But treat it as a combo piece, not as fodder. It has no substitute anywhere in the pool: one sacrifice to Phyrexian Altar or Warren Soultrader refunds exactly one mana, and Gravecrawler is the only body that comes back for {B} with no other gate. Reassembling Skeleton costs {1}{B}. Feed it to the commander for a card and you have eaten a kill for a draw step.

Bastion of Remembrance is the other load-bearing permanent, and it is the one you cannot protect. It is the drain that loops in three of the four verified kills, and it is an enchantment — Lightning Greaves, Supernatural Stamina and Malakir Rebirth all protect a creature. Goldfish draws it by turn ten in 16.7% of games unassisted, 66.2% with a tutor, mean draw turn 3.641. Hold it until the turn it converts.

Be straight about what you are at Rule 0, because honesty here costs you nothing and buys real goodwill. Bracket floor 4, Optimized, forced independently by four Game Changers (Ancient Tomb, Demonic Tutor, Necropotence, Vampiric Tutor) and by eleven two-card infinite records; 32 combo lines fully contained; five tutors. Then say the part that actually matters: four rules-verified kills, two of them unbounded, each ending all four opponents at once. Nobody can convert that sentence into a turn number, and you have told them the truth.

Mikaeus is your loudest card and you should let him be. He is half of seven of the eleven two-card infinite records the bracket report names, so he draws exile on sight from anyone who reads. Stack 010 — the version that is checker-passed — is the one kill that can run out before it finishes: 39 activations needed against 59 the mandatory draw permits, margin 20 clean and at most 25. He is a magnificent lightning rod attached to your slowest line.

One trap inside that line, verified and easy to walk into: Viscera Seer's free outlet is not a free bonus mid-loop. Stack 010 prices it at roughly 34 of the 39 activations you need. Save the Seer for the finish.

Your commander is the other thing you should be pleased to trade. Stacks 009, 011 and 012 name him nowhere. He lands on turn four in 7,220 of 10,000 games, mean cast turn 4.294, and 91.1% by turn six — so cast him on curve, draw four or five cards with him, and let a removal spell take him. Do not hold mana to protect him and do not mulligan toward him. strategy:multiplayer.commander-insurance gives you the permission in as many words: against light-interaction pods, "skip the insurance, pay the tax, rebuild."

Sequence so the scariest piece is last. strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window is blunt about the reason — "sequence the scariest piece last so the deflection budget lasts until the turn you take it" — and strategy:tempo.sequencing gives you the timing: commit "at the end step before your own turn so the table's chances to respond are spent." Fodder, outlet and Gravecrawler go down early and cheaply. Exquisite Blood and the drain wait.

Now the distinction inside those four that decides when you go. Stacks 009 and 011 are unbounded: the board returns to an identical state every iteration, so the count is never a resource and you choose each step. Stacks 012 and 010 are countdowns to a fixed number.

An unbounded loop you can stop. Take the drains you want, keep priority, and the engine is intact next turn — 009 dips to 39 life and refunds, 011 pays nothing at all. That is why those two are the ones you may attempt into a live table.

Stack 012 you cannot stop. Neither Exquisite Blood nor South Wind Avatar says "may", so once that first life gain resolves the game runs the count for you. It ends at drain 40 because that is where the pod ends: "the sequence is not one that could be repeated indefinitely" and there is a way to stop. Lethal is the loop's off switch.

So 012 is your one all-in, and it is the one that can be raced or cut mid-count. Each drain is a separate resolution with priority in between, and an opponent who answers either half at drain 25 leaves you holding twenty-five drains of progress and no engine. The seats that survive have watched a public countdown aimed at all of them.

Take that as licence rather than fear. strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window sets the bar at a win attempt that "doesn't need to resolve fully to leave you ahead", and a half-run 012 clears it on raw life — the full run gains you 40. It just clears it in the loudest way you own. Start it when the table's interaction is spent, not when it is merely quiet.

Stack 010 is the countdown that can run out on its own, and the resource it spends is your library. The 59 activations the mandatory draw permits are that board's 59 cards; your own draws earlier in the game come off the top of them. Count your library before you start the Mikaeus line, never during.

When the configuration is live, go, and go without apology. Two of these attempts are extraordinarily cheap to make: stack 009's ledger is life-neutral per iteration, dipping to 39 and refunding, and stack 011 pays nothing at all and gains you a life every time round. pivot-window asks you to "prefer win attempts that leave a rebuilt position if they fail." These do. Count the table's open mana, assume every held answer appears, and then take it.

Last thing, and it is the discipline that keeps you honest. There is no single number for "how often does this deck assemble something lethal," and you must not invent one. The simulator scores each requirement group on its own, so nothing in it expresses "any kill assembled." Quote the four separately: 1.1% unassisted and 18.0% with a tutor for stack 009's shape by turn ten, 0.5% / 12.3% for stack 011's, 6.9% / 42.5% for Exquisite Blood's, 4.6% / 33.7% for the Mikaeus line. Adding them is a lie you would tell yourself, and this deck is good enough that you never need to.
matchups:
Assign your role first, then re-ask after every board change. strategy:whos-the-beatdown gives the operational test — "who has inevitability? — whoever loses the long game must be the beatdown" — and in a fair pod that is not you. You are the control deck with a combo clock. Its Commander correction is the one you will actually use every turn: "you can be the beatdown against one opponent and the control against another in the same turn cycle; assign per-threat, not per-game."

SWEEPER CONTROL is a matchup you should be visibly happy to be in. A wrath is a payoff here. Bastion of Remembrance, Zulaport Cutthroat and The Meathook Massacre each bill every opponent when a creature you control dies, and Blood Artist bills one seat whenever any creature dies at all — so their sweeper pays you four ways per body it takes. Your rebuild is structural rather than held: Reassembling Skeleton returns for {1}{B} forever, Gravecrawler recasts for {B} while a Zombie is out, and Bitterblossom and Black Market Connections make a body a turn without spending a card.

Better than that — a wrath does not touch a single one of your kills. Every verified line's critical permanents are noncreature: Bastion of Remembrance, Exquisite Blood, Phyrexian Altar. The board they blow up is the decoration.

Deploy fodder freely and hold the payoff. strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math tells you to "commit exactly as much as wins before it arrives, no further," and here what wins is a configuration, not a body count, so there is nothing to overextend into.

Plumb the Forbidden is what flips this matchup outright. Two mana at instant speed, sacrifice any number of creatures as an additional cost, copy itself once per creature — their wrath announcement becomes your draw step, and every sacrifice also fires whatever drain you have down. Hold two mana whenever a control player untaps with four or more open; assume a sweeper deck keeps its sweeper mana up.

The real exposure in this seat is the one card class you cannot answer. Feed the Swarm is the only card in the 99 that destroys a noncreature permanent an opponent controls, and it reads "creature or enchantment" — so a resolved artifact aimed at you is unanswerable, and deck-audit measures interaction-breadth at 2 classes answered against a target of 5, naming artifact, graveyard and land as uncovered. Goldfish has Feed the Swarm in hand by turn ten in 17.3% of games unassisted, 66.9% with a tutor. strategy:deckbuilding.interaction-suite names the standard you are missing: "Breadth before depth."

STAX AND TAX is the matchup this deck is quietly built for, and the reason is verified rather than argued. Three of the four kills need essentially no external mana once assembled. Stack 009's Treasure "exactly funds the next cast." Stack 011's Phyrexian Altar "is a mana ability, so it never used the stack," refunds its own {B} every iteration, and pays no life at any point. Stack 012 spends nothing at all. And your commander's ability costs no mana in the first place.

So recount your hand under a tax, not your board. strategy:threat-assessment.resource-denial is right that taxes "attack the velocity math directly," but a loop that is already running is not in your hand. Your vulnerable window is deployment, not operation.

Name your outs early, as that section demands — "the removal or velocity that breaks the piece that beats *you*, not the scariest piece." Two things genuinely beat you: graveyard hate, and a noncreature lock permanent. Against a Cursed Totem or a Pithing Needle pointed at your commander, your outlets are the noncreatures — Ashnod's Altar, Phyrexian Altar, Blasting Station, Phyrexian Tower — and Phyrexian Altar is a kill piece anyway. Against an artifact lock piece you have no answer, so race it: you are the beatdown in that seat, and the fastest of your kills has a mean assembly turn of 5.301.

GRAVEYARD HATE deserves its own heading, because it hits this deck asymmetrically and knowing which half is live is worth a whole game. Stacks 009 and 011 cast Gravecrawler out of the graveyard every single iteration, so a Rest in Peace effect blanks both unbounded loops outright. Stack 012 touches no graveyard whatsoever. Stack 010 runs on undying returns from the battlefield.

The read under hate is therefore simple and you should make it instantly: abandon the recursion shape and tutor for Exquisite Blood plus a body reading "Whenever you gain life, each opponent loses 1 life." That is also your fastest line — 6.9% assembled by turn ten unassisted, 42.5% with a tutor, mean turn 5.301, against 1.1% and 0.5% for the recursion kills. One caution to carry: stack 012 verified that pairing on South Wind Avatar, whose own dies-trigger lifegain starts the loop. Marauding Blight-Priest and Starscape Cleric carry the identical drain text but gain no life by themselves, so they need an external lifegain event and they need a stack scenario before you call them the same line.

You are not defenceless against their graveyard either. Bojuka Bog exiles a graveyard as it enters — a free hit off a land drop, so play it on the turn it costs them something rather than the turn it is convenient.

AGGRO makes you the pod's stabiliser, and you have the tools to enjoy it. Four sweepers (Black Sun's Zenith, Toxic Deluge, The Meathook Massacre, Soul Snuffers), 13 interaction copies, 28 creatures to chump or eat, and Grave Pact turning your own engine into a table-wide edict every time a body dies. That is strategy:multiplayer.asymmetry's whole request — "Your cards should do something to all three seats or win the game."

Be precise about which sweeper feeds you. Black Sun's Zenith places actual -1/-1 counters, and stack 006 verified that counters put on a creature already on the battlefield do trigger Nest of Scarabs. Toxic Deluge and The Meathook Massacre apply -X/-X until end of turn and trigger nothing. Stack 013 settled how the Nest counts — the number of creatures you touch sets the number of triggers, and the counters on each of them set that trigger's "that many" — and explicitly declined to resolve a Zenith at X greater than 1, so do not promise yourself a specific token count off a big one.

Point the commander's counters at opponents' creatures whenever a legal target exists. Stacks 002 and 003 both measured an opposing 2-toughness creature EXTENDING the engine by two activations rather than bounding it — free removal and free fuel in the same habit, costing you nothing.

And stop defending your life total a turn too early. Stack 011 ends you at 80 having paid nothing; stack 012 gains you 40. The costs that actually drain you are Necropotence, Bitterblossom, Black Market Connections, City of Brass and Warren Soultrader's "Pay 1 life." strategy:life-as-resource sets the discipline: spend early points cheaply, and switch "from spending to defending one turn before it matters, not one after."

COMBO is your hardest seat and you should meet it head-on rather than hedge. You have no counterspells; your instant-speed answers are Deadly Rollick, Fatal Push and Snuff Out, all pointed at creatures, against a kill that may not use one. That is the price strategy:critical-mass names — "interaction slots are the price of the engine" — and you pay it with speed.

So hold nothing back. strategy:threat-assessment.answer-economy carries the clause that governs this seat: "held answers rot — against combo, or lethal already on board, the last profitable moment is now." Deadly Rollick is free while you control your commander, which is most turns from turn four onward. Spend it on the enabler the moment it lands.

Then race with the line you can finish, not the one you would prefer. strategy:resource-hedging.playing-to-outs: "identify the card or event that saves you and play as if it's coming." Your enabler classes are deep — a drain 82.4% by turn ten, a free sacrifice outlet 77.9%, renewable fodder 73.6%, an ignition source 73.1%, engine mana 61.9%, each rising to between 85% and 94% once a tutor is involved. The pieces show up. Your job is to have the right two of them on the battlefield on a turn the table has already spent its mana, and this deck gives you four different ways to be right.
